Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-03
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: 58 minutes (scheduled 60)
Attendees: Lina Torres (Redwood AE), Arjun Patel (Redwood SE), Sam O'Neill (Redwood Infra), Mark DeSantis (CTO - Silverline), Priya Rao (ML Engineer), Dan Weber (SRE), Sofia Cruz (Product)
Recording ID: fireflies-20260303-7f4a

Summary (auto): technical deep dive on KV cache eviction and paging behavior with Silverline's long-context workloads. Discussed root causes for unexpected evictions, paging to host memory, effects of prefix reuse, batching/throughput tradeoffs, and on-prem/VPC implications. Agreed next steps include benchmark run and sharing detailed docs.

Transcript:
[00:00] Lina Torres: All right everyone thanks for joining. We're going to do a deep dive into the KV cache behavior you saw in the last run; Arjun is going to lead on the runtime and eviction patterns. uh quick roll call?
[00:10] Mark DeSantis: Hey Mark here, Priya, Dan, Sofia with me.
[00:14] Priya Rao: Priya on the line.
[00:16] Dan Weber: Dan, SRE.
[00:18] Arjun Patel: Arjun, Redwood SE. Thanks y'all.
[00:20] Lina Torres: Cool. We'll try to keep it technical. Arjun, you want to kick us off with your view of the eviction symptoms?
[00:26] Arjun Patel: Yeah thanks. So from our end we saw two main symptoms: one, frequent KV eviction at sequence lengths below what we'd expect given your cache size; two, when eviction happens there's a lot of paging activity - by paging I mean spill-to-host slower path - and that spikes latencies for tokens following the eviction.
[00:45] Arjun Patel: Important context: Silverline's workload reuses many prefixes across sessions, but also has long tail sessions with sequences up to 32k tokens. In our profiler the eviction is correlated with high concurrency + uneven prefix reuse where a few sessions have huge KV growth and push others out.
[01:05] Priya Rao: quick interject - when you say "KV growth" are you counting per-request kv cache or shared per-VM? We're running the hosted variant with dedicated nodes but per-customer pool.
[01:16] Arjun Patel: Good call. It's per-inference runtime instance (per worker) not global across the pool. So if you have many concurrent requests landing on the same worker, you can exhaust that worker's KV memory. That leads to our eviction policy kicking in.
[01:29] Dan Weber: We're seeing errors in our traces: sudden token latency jumps around certain timestamps, then requests get re-tried by our client and sometimes we see duplicates. Could that be eviction causing generation restarts?
[01:40] Sam O'Neill: Possibly. If eviction clears needed prefix KV, the runtime may need to regenerate KV for the next segments and that looks like extra work and latency. Also depending on retry logic the client may resend inputs and cause duplicated state.
[01:50] Mark DeSantis: So is the cache global per VCPU or per model shard? I'm trying to map this to our capacity planning.
[01:58] Arjun Patel: Per worker process which maps to a subset of GPU resources - effectively per-model-shard process. We tried to map your traces to specific workers and saw a hot worker receiving disproportionate traffic.
[02:10] Priya Rao: Hotshard - right. We do use sticky routing currently based on session id, which explains it. We didn't realize one session type would be so heavy.
[02:18] Arjun Patel: Sticky routing + uneven prefix reuse makes it worse. If one session reuses very long prefixes, the worker KV grows and evicts other active prefixes.
[02:27] Lina Torres: Let's go through eviction policy options. Arjun?
[02:30] Arjun Patel: The default policy uses an LRU-ish TTL combined with size windows. It tries to keep KV for active prefixes but if memory pressure hits a hard threshold it will evict least recently used segments. We also have a soft threshold where we attempt to compress or quantize cached KV for older segments (this is the paging-friendly path). Paging is our fallback where we move KV to host DRAM for quick retrieval rather than discarding it entirely. But that path is slower and increases tail latency.
[02:58] Priya Rao: The paging you mentioned - is that GPU-to-host or within GPU memory management? How much slower?
[03:05] Arjun Patel: It's GPU-to-host spill. Latency penalty varies, but in our measurements a spill+refill adds ~50-150ms per refill depending on the size and PCIe vs NVLink topology. With NVLink it can be lower; with PCIe it can be worse. If you have frequent small spills it aggregates into significant tail.
[03:23] Dan Weber: Our infra is multi-az with PCIe instances (older gen). That aligns with the spikes.
[03:29] Mark DeSantis: Could quantization help the KV growth? We already quantize weights for inference.
[03:35] Arjun Patel: Yes, quantized KV formats reduce per-token KV footprint - for example int8 vs fp16 can be 2x reduction; 4-bit formats even more but with reconstruction cost. We have runtime-supported quantized KV caching profiles that trade accuracy and refill CPU cost. For some workloads with heavy prefix reuse quantization plus async background rehydrate reduces tail significantly.
[03:58] Priya Rao: What's "async background rehydrate"?
[04:00] Arjun Patel: It's when, after a page-to-host, the runtime spawns a lower-priority refill to warm GPU KV before requests hit it again. It amortizes cost but requires headroom and scheduling support.
[04:10] Sofia Cruz: Sounds like that needs infra support; can that run on different worker nodes?
[04:14] Sam O'Neill: We don't move data between nodes easily because KV is tied to model state in the process. But you can run a pre-warm worker that reconstructs prefix KV from stored traces or from host-cache, depends on your setup. For Dedicated or Private deployments you can tune this with our pre-warm hooks.
[04:30] Mark DeSantis: Ok let's talk prefix reuse. We expected reuse to help cache hit rate - but you're saying uneven reuse can hurt others. How do we mitigate?
[04:40] Arjun Patel: A few tactics: 1) route sessions to multiple workers (round-robin) to spread hot prefixes; 2) size your worker KV capacity higher (bigger instance or more GPU memory per worker); 3) enable per-customer dedicated pool with more consistent load; 4) tune eviction thresholds to favor longer-lived prefixes if reuse is high. Also consider prefix compaction: if many sessions share near-identical prefixes, we can canonicalize storage so multiple sessions reference the same cache entries rather than duplicate. That's an internal optimization we can enable in pilot.
[05:10] Priya Rao: Canonicalize - any correctness risk with token offsets? We have slight prompt variations.
[05:15] Arjun Patel: Small prompt variations that change tokenization offsets cause separate KV entries. Canonicalization requires normalizing prefixes (e.g., whitespace, special tokens) or defining similarity heuristics. It's lossy if the variation affects model activations; we only recommend it when prefixes are near-identical by tokenization.
[05:30] Dan Weber: You mentioned routing changes. We currently use sticky routing because session state matters. If we round-robin we risk losing short-term locality for sessions - tradeoffs?
[05:40] Arjun Patel: For sessions that truly require sticky runtime state (e.g., streaming chat with cache growth) you keep sticky. For request/response patterns where prefix reuse is common but session isn't continuous, we can use affinity windows: route new requests to different workers but attach a short TTL affinity to avoid hotness. It's a middle ground.
[05:56] Mark DeSantis: Is there telemetry we can look at to identify hot workers and prefix duplication?
[06:01] Arjun Patel: Yes, we can provide per-worker KV memory usage traces, per-prefix hit rates, and a mapping of session IDs to workers. We'll share a dashboard prototype.
[06:10] Priya Rao: On the paging topic: is there a config to increase the soft threshold or disable paging (just evict)? Which is better?
[06:18] Arjun Patel: Disabling paging means more evictions and more regen cost; enabling paging keeps state but adds latency on refill. If tail latency is critical you may prefer evict+pre-warm for known prefixes. If correctness of continuation is more important, paging avoids complete loss. There's also a hybrid where we page large/old entries and evict tiny ones. We can tune heuristics by token span and last-access time.
[06:42] Sofia Cruz: For on-prem / VPC concerns - any difference for Private deployment?
[06:46] Sam O'Neill: On Private, you control instance selection. If you provision NVLink-connected GPUs and larger host memory, paging cost goes down. Also, Dedicated pools let you size for these long-context workloads. The runtime is the same; you just get more knobs on infra.
[07:00] Mark DeSantis: We do have an on-prem proof-of-concept coming up. Good to know.
[07:03] Priya Rao: Arjun, can you show us the specific traces you pulled?
[07:06] Arjun Patel: Yeah I pulled two traces - one where eviction caused a refill and a second where a hot worker spilled repeatedly. [screen share narration starts but transcription auto-misses some content]
[07:20] Arjun Patel: (screen) Here's a timeline: you can see KV usage per worker, sudden jump at 10:12:22, then eviction window, then paging spikes. Notice the correlation with a 32k sequence generation job that started around the same time.
[07:35] Priya Rao: That 32k was an overnight batch job that we maybe didn't isolate. We thought batching would be okay.
[07:40] Arjun Patel: Large single sessions like that are the primary cause - even if they're rare, they cause big KV growth. For batching: larger batch sizes increase concurrent KV pressure since per-request KV is stored until completion. Batching is great for throughput but needs bigger memory headroom.
[07:55] Dan Weber: So recommendation: isolate heavy batch jobs to separate pool or schedule low-concurrency windows?
[08:01] Arjun Patel: Exactly. Either separate pool or use lower-concurrency workers for those large sequences. We can also enable batch-aware eviction where very large batch entries are treated differently.
[08:12] Mark DeSantis: About retries - we observed duplicate token sequences, how to avoid client-level retries causing more pressure?
[08:19] Sam O'Neill: Client retries should be idempotent at the RPC layer but you can add a dedupe token to avoid duplicate generation. Also the runtime exposes a short-lived in-flight dedupe for requests with same session+offset. We'll share our best-practices doc.
[08:32] Priya Rao: Are there knobs in the model runtime for compacting KV entries? Like delta-compression?
[08:37] Arjun Patel: We have two approaches: quantized representation (reduces size) and delta/fragment compaction for contiguous token spans. Delta compaction works well when activations between adjacent tokens are similar; it's workload dependent. It can add CPU cost to reconstruct.
[08:50] Mark DeSantis: Ok can you summarize immediate mitigation steps we can do in our account today?
[08:55] Arjun Patel: Sure: 1) Identify and isolate large long-context jobs to separate worker pool. 2) Increase worker memory or use instance types with larger GPU memory for your busiest pool. 3) Tune routing from sticky to affinity windows to spread hot prefixes. 4) Enable runtime quantized KV profiles for your workload and test for quality regression. 5) Share logs/traces and we'll run a targeted benchmark.
[09:18] Lina Torres: We'll also send the architecture doc and eviction tuning guide. Dan and Arjun will coordinate the benchmark.
[09:25] Priya Rao: One last question - how does model versioning affect KV reuse after rollouts? We do frequent small rollouts.
[09:33] Arjun Patel: If the model weights change, KV entries generally are invalidated because internal activations diverge. For small patch rollouts we can do compatibility checks; in practice we purge KV on major model updates. Rolling A/B with shared warmers reduces cold start impact.
[09:48] Mark DeSantis: Good to know.
[09:50] Sofia Cruz: Anything else on quantization and throughput tradeoffs?
[09:53] Arjun Patel: Tradeoffs: lower-bit KV reduces memory and can improve throughput because more in-GPU fits; but CPU reconstruction cost and small numeric differences can change outputs slightly. We'll provide benchmark matrix.
[10:05] Dan Weber: We'll send logs today.
[10:08] Lina Torres: Great. Let's recap quick.
[10:10] Lina Torres: Recap: action items - Arjun will run benchmark with Silverline dataset, Dan to send logs/traces, Lina to send pricing + docs, Priya to share prompt sets. We'll reconvene after benchmark. Anything else?
[10:22] Mark DeSantis: No, thanks everyone. Good call.
[10:25] Lina Torres: Thanks all; we'll follow up in email with links to docs and dashboards. End.

Notes and references: mentions of NVLink vs PCIe, quantization (int8/4-bit), paging-to-host DRAM, sticky routing vs affinity windows, prefix canonicalization, pre-warm hooks, batch-aware eviction.
